description: Hi, I’m Krithik, a student forming a team for the "Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions" challenge.
summary:
Aegis-EIMO is an astronaut health-monitoring prototype designed for deep-space missions, where communication delays make immediate medical advice from Earth impossible. It brings health information into a clickable body map, helping crew members understand changes in their eyes, cognitive performance, cardiovascular system, and musculoskeletal health. Instead of relying only on population-wide thresholds, the design compares daily measurements with each astronaut’s preflight baseline to highlight changes over time.
The platform combines reaction and near-vision checks with guided pulse measurement, sleep and mood logging, and delay-aware symptom triage. Its medical-locker workflow connects potential next steps with available onboard supplies and prepares structured information for flight surgeons on Earth. A NASA DONKI integration provides space-weather context without claiming to measure personal radiation dose.
Our goal is to make health information useful when the crew must act locally: recognize a change, understand its limits, and prepare a better-informed response. Aegis-EIMO is a decision-support concept, not a diagnostic device or a replacement for trained medical judgment.
details:
Purpose and workflow

Aegis-EIMO stands for Earth-Independent Medical Operations. Our project addresses a practical problem in deep-space health care: a crew member may need help before a message can travel to Earth and a response can return. The design brings daily health checks, individual trends, symptom intake, and communication planning into one astronaut-facing interface.

The home screen is a clickable human silhouette. Selecting the eyes, brain, heart and vascular system, or bones opens the relevant measurements, trends, explanations of spaceflight risks, and follow-up guidance. Radiation appears separately because it is an environmental hazard, not an organ. This connects a reading with its context rather than displaying isolated numbers.

Personal baselines and daily checks

The baseline engine compares reaction-test results, near-vision scores, pulse, and sleep entries with an astronaut’s own preflight measurements. Its purpose is to highlight gradual changes that a single population-wide threshold could miss. Pre-seeded mission histories are labeled as simulated; a trend flag is not a diagnosis.

The planned daily workflow includes a three-minute reaction test, a screen-calibrated tumbling-E near-vision check, guided pulse counting or manual pulse entry, and sleep and mood logging. Reaction performance is considered alongside reported alertness and recent sleep. A 15-second test is included for demonstrations only and is not equivalent to the longer assessment. Readiness categories use team-defined cutoffs, not NASA-validated clearance for spacewalks or docking. The vision check tracks near-vision change and prompts further assessment; it does not diagnose Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS).

Medical support under communication delay

The symptom workflow is designed around common in-flight complaints and an example onboard medical inventory. It connects a reported problem with available supplies and follow-up questions while showing the communication delay to Earth. A structured packet gathers information for ground medical staff, aiming to reduce avoidable back-and-forth. The prototype supports information gathering and review, not unsupervised diagnosis or prescribing. Established emergency procedures take priority over waiting for a ground response.

The space-weather module is designed to use NASA’s DONKI event reports. It provides context for reviewing mission radiation procedures, not a measurement of astronaut exposure or a location-specific hazard prediction. A historical storm can be replayed for demonstrations, with the replay clearly labeled. DONKI alone does not establish a crew member’s radiation dose or determine the appropriate operational response.

Benefits, creativity, and intended impact

The central idea is to connect the body map, personal baseline, and communication-delay workflow. A crew member can move from “what changed?” to “what information do we need next?” without navigating unrelated dashboards. An interactive reaction test makes fatigue monitoring tangible during a demonstration, while daily reminders and cooperative streaks encourage consistent logging without ranking crewmates.

Our intended impact is better-organized health information and more informed communication when real-time telemedicine is unavailable. We do not claim that the prototype has demonstrated improved clinical outcomes or that its screening tools replace medical evaluation.

Technical approach and design considerations

The source design specifies a modular, client-side application with local persistent storage, a clickable SVG or WebGL anatomical interface, pre-seeded longitudinal demonstration data, a communication-delay countdown, and a NASA DONKI API connection. Local storage is intended to keep core checks and saved records usable during communication outages; live space-weather updates still require connectivity.

We considered limited onboard supplies, intermittent connectivity, sensitive health information, measurement quality, and the need to distinguish observations from simulation. Camera-based pulse estimation and predictive bone-loss modeling are outside the core design to avoid fragile measurements and unsupported precision.
